subject: sociology
title: Crime & Deviance: Realism, Feminism & Globalisation
welcome_lead: Take crime seriously — and ask who is left out of the picture.
meta_desc: A-Level Sociology crime: left realism right realism feminism globalisation.
final_note: Modern theories combine structure, agency and global flows.

concepts.def: Lea & Young — relative deprivation, subculture, marginalisation.
Wilson & Kelling — broken windows, rational choice.
Young's four corners: state, offender, victim, public.
Heidensohn — women under control at home, work, public.
Castells — global crime networks, transnational trafficking.
Bauman — instability driving new crime patterns.

walkthroughs.body_html: Right realism (Wilson 1975) sees crime as rational choice; advocates situational crime prevention and broken windows policing (Wilson & Kelling 1982). Left realism (Lea & Young 1984) blames relative deprivation, subculture and marginalisation — solution is multi-agency response.

Official statistics: men commit ~80% of UK crime. Heidensohn (1985): women are over-controlled in home (domestic role), workplace (sexual harassment) and public space (fear of male violence). Carlen (1988): women break the gender deal. Adler (1975) liberation thesis — women's crime rises with equality.

Castells (1998): global criminal economy worth ~$1 trillion. Networks transport drugs, people and weapons. Taylor (1997): deregulated capitalism creates new opportunities for white-collar crime. Beck (1992): risk society — global risks like terrorism and cybercrime defy borders.
